title: Londoner v. Denver (1908)
summary: Owners subjected to individualized paving assessments had to receive an opportunity to support their objections before the assessments became final.
notes: Justice Moody wrote for the Court; the key language is verbatim: "a hearing in its very essence demands that he who is entitled to it shall have the right to support his allegations by argument however brief, and, if need be, by proof, however informal."

sections.Parties: Landowners in Denver sought to discharge their properties from tax liens for paving an adjoining street. Denver defended the assessment procedure under its municipal charter.
sections.Material Facts: The charter separated authorization of the improvement from the later allocation of its cost to benefited lots. After the work was completed, the public-works board proposed particular assessments and the clerk invited written objections, promising they would be heard before final assessment. The owners timely objected that the district and allocation were arbitrary, that some assessed land received inadequate benefit, and that the work and charges were improper. The council then met specially without notice to them, characterized their objections as denying the city’s power to assess rather than challenging apportionment, and approved the charges without allowing argument or proof.
sections.Procedural History: The state trial court granted relief to the owners; Colorado’s supreme court reversed and directed judgment for the city. On writ of error, the United States Supreme Court accepted the state court’s construction of the charter and addressed the federal due-process objection. It reversed, holding the assessment void. The Chief Justice and Justice Holmes dissented without reasons reproduced in the excerpt.
sections.Issue: Did filing written objections supply due process when a subordinate local body determined which owners owed a special assessment and in what amount, and no later court could hear the merits of those objections?
sections.Holding: The assessment violated the Fourteenth Amendment because the owners lacked a meaningful opportunity to support their objections before liability became irrevocably fixed. They were entitled to discharge of the resulting liens. The Constitution did not separately require a hearing on the preliminary decision to undertake the improvement or the council’s determination that the required petition existed.
sections.Reasoning: The Court separated general authorization from the later individualized imposition of liability. The legislature could authorize the improvement without owner participation, provided the assessment itself received constitutionally adequate process. Once a subordinate body decided whether, on whom, and in what amount the cost would fall, affected owners needed notice and an opportunity to support allegations through argument and, when necessary, proof. A complete judicial trial was unnecessary; brief argument and informal evidence could suffice. Written objections alone were inadequate here because the council never afforded the promised opportunity to be heard and state law foreclosed a later judicial challenge to the allocation. The decision protects a hearing on individualized facts rather than requiring personal participation in every governmental decision affecting property.
